sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** The piece has no main image, and the copy calls for one. The subhead (120–716, y≈380–440) promises "one honest picture of the next five days", but nothing on the screen shows that picture. Everything sits in the top two-thirds, and the band below the button (y≈540–800, full width) is blank white. The right half beside the headline (x≈950–1160) is also empty. A visitor has to take "the week your team actually works" on trust. They never see the week view that would prove it and show how this differs from their own calendar or ticket board. That turns a specific promise into a claim anyone could make. Fix: put the product's week view (tickets, meetings and leave on one five-day picture) in the hero, either below the button or to the right of the text. Then the image is the "honest picture" and the headline says why it matters, without either one repeating the other. If an image is meant to be there and didn't load, this finding goes away; check the live page. This is taste (the catalog entry has no approved source), argued on common sense: a product page that promises a picture should show it. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The page has one message and one ask. The headline names the job (planning a team's real week), the subhead names the inputs (tickets, meetings, leave) and the unit (the next five days), and there is a single button. A stranger can say what this is in one sentence within seconds.
- It looks like one piece. There's one sans family in a few weights, near-black and slate-grey text, and a single blue that is used only on the call to action. Nothing on the page is decoration, so every element does a job.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The empty band under the button and the empty right side may be a hero image or product shot that hadn't loaded, or a scroll animation that hadn't run, when the screenshot was taken. Check in a live browser whether anything renders at y≈540–800 or to the right of the headline.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea together)

Walk notes (working):

First read: the eye lands on the two-line headline (x 120–945, y 180–345), drops to the grey subhead, then to the blue "Start a free trial" button. This looks like a SaaS landing hero for team leads.

What matters first:
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? Yes. The headline is about 80 px and very heavy, roughly four times the next size.
- Can you tell each level apart, with no near-duplicate sizes? Yes. I count about four sizes: headline (~80 px), subhead (~21 px regular grey), logo (~20 px bold dark), nav and button (~16 px). The logo and subhead are close in size but sit in different places and differ in weight and colour, so they don't collide.
- Do headings also differ in weight, form, or colour? Yes. The headline is heavy and near-black, and the subhead is regular and mid-grey.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline is the clear place to start.** "Plan the week your team actually works" (x 120–945, y 180–345) is about four times the size of anything else and is set heavy and near-black. Nothing competes with it, so the eye knows where to begin.
- **Each level after the headline differs in more than size.** The subhead (y 380–440) is regular weight and mid-grey. The button (x 120–289, y 478–530) is the only saturated colour on the page. So the order is headline, then explanation, then action, and you can see it at a glance even though the subhead and nav sizes are only a few pixels apart.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I critiqued the arrangement section only. I found one major problem: all the content sits in the upper left, and the right side and bottom of the screen are empty.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?" and "Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?"**
   - **Where:** Everything with weight sits in the upper left, from about x 120–945 and y 180–530: the large dark headline, the subhead and the blue button. To the right of x≈950 (about 40% of the width) and below y≈530 (about a third of the height), the screen is empty. The only thing out there is the small nav text at the top right.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The space is gathered, not scattered, but it doesn't look chosen. The empty right side reads as a gap where a product picture failed to load or was never designed. That makes the frame tip toward the top left. The eye goes headline → subhead → button and then has nowhere to go. Nothing on the right holds it, and nothing at the bottom hints there is more below.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception* ("Balance"): a heavy side needs a counterweight. Tschichold and Müller-Brockmann: large empty areas with no explanation are a fault.
   - **Fix direction:**
     - Give the right side a counterweight that does the page's job, such as a view of the actual week plan (that's what the headline promises).
     - Or make the emptiness clearly intended. Scale the headline block up and move it lower so the open space reads as a frame around it.
     - Either way, let the next section start above the bottom edge, so the eye has a way to go on.
   - **Kind:** Defect. It costs the page the chance to show the product, and it looks unfinished.
   - **Weight:** Major.

**What's working.**
- **One strict left edge.** The logo, headline, subhead and button all sit at x≈120, and the nav's right edge at x≈1160 mirrors that margin. The block reads as one firm column with nothing slightly off. Keep that edge if you add a picture.
- **Spacing shows the order.** There are about 140 px from the nav to the headline, about 40 px from the headline to the subhead, and about 50 px from the subhead to the button. The nav reads as separate, and the headline, subhead and call to action read as one unit, in that order.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (visual weight balances; empty space gathered and deliberate)

The text section of the Weekplan hero page mostly holds up. The one problem is the headline's spacing, which is too loose.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Are large headings set with tighter letter and word spacing than the text?** No. The headline "Plan the week your / team actually works" (about x 120–945, y 180–345, cap height around 65 px) looks tracked out, not tightened. Look at the gaps inside "week", "actually" and "works", and at the wide word spaces between "the week your". At this size the line reads as a row of separate words rather than one firm statement. It looks airy where it should look solid, and that weakens the opening claim the whole page rests on.
   - **Why:** Space between letters and words looks wider as type gets bigger, so headlines need tighter spacing than text. Bringhurst §2.1.1 says the spacing of words can be tightened at larger sizes. Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*, says larger sizes need proportionally less word space. Lupton, *Thinking with Type*, p. 80, says large letters usually need their letter spacing adjusted.
   - **Fix:** Remove any positive tracking. Set the headline at the face's default spacing or slightly tighter, around −1% to −2% for a sans this heavy, and tighten the word spaces to match. Lupton warns that negative tracking should be used sparingly, so stop as soon as letters start to touch.
   - Convention. Weight: minor. The page still works, but the headline would look noticeably firmer.

**What's working.**
- **The subhead:** At about x 120–716, y 383–437, it runs about 62 characters per line. That's inside the comfortable 45–75 range (Bringhurst). It is set at about 20 px with relaxed leading, so the one sentence explaining the product is easy to read in a single pass.
- **One type family:** The page uses a single sans in a few clearly separate sizes and weights: the bold headline, the regular grey subhead, the bold button label and the medium nav. Nothing nearly matches anything else, so each piece of text has an obvious job.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (large headings spaced tighter than text).

sections.report:
I critiqued the Interface section and found one problem: the page gives a visitor who isn't ready to start a trial nothing else to do. Everything else in the section passes.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a logo, three nav links (Product, Pricing, Sign in) and one filled button ("Start a free trial").

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** No.
   - **Where:** the whole hero offers one action, the button at about x 120–289, y 478–530, and it asks the visitor to commit. Below it, rows about 560 to 800 are blank across the full width.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** someone arriving cold reads "one honest picture of the next five days" and wants to see that picture. Nothing shows it, and nothing near the button offers a lower-commitment step like "See how it works" or a product preview. The button also doesn't answer the questions people have just before clicking: how long the trial is, and whether it needs a card. A visitor who isn't ready to commit has to go hunting in the nav (Product) or leave.
   - **Why:** the catalog entry is Tognazzini's "Anticipation", which is off the approved reading list. So this is my own judgement on common-sense grounds: a hero should put the information the visitor came for, or the next step they're ready for, right where they already are.
   - **Fix:**
     - Put the thing the subline promises (a real week view) into the empty lower area or beside the headline.
     - Or add one quieter secondary action next to the button, such as a text link to a demo or tour, styled clearly below the primary.
     - Add a short line under the button stating the trial terms, for example "14 days, no card".
   - **Kind and weight:** taste, major. It decides whether undecided visitors take any next step at all.

**What's working.**
- **Clear primary action.** There is exactly one: the saturated blue filled button is the only coloured element on the page, so there's no doubt what the page wants you to do. "Sign in" is correctly kept as a plain nav link rather than competing as a second button.
- **Conventional nav.** Logo on the left, links on the right, and Sign in last. This is the pattern visitors expect from comparable SaaS sites, so the nav takes no effort to read.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Focus and hover states:** none are shown for the nav links or the button. Check in a browser that each has a visible focus indicator at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast, and that the button has a hover or pressed state.
- **Nav link click area:** whether it extends beyond the roughly 16 px text height. It passes on spacing either way, but a larger padded area would be better.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (puts what the user needs next in front of them), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
